title: God's People Marked and Sheltered
overview: In a pause before the last seal is opened, God marks his people as his own, and John sees a vast rescued crowd at rest in God's presence.

parts.label: Winds held back (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Four angels at the four corners of the earth, meaning the whole world, hold back winds that are about to do harm until another angel marks God's servants on their foreheads. A seal showed ownership and protection, as with the mark that spared the faithful in Ezekiel 9, though readers differ on whether it shields them from harm or keeps them safe as God's own through it.

parts.label: 144,000 from Israel's tribes (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: Twelve thousand from each of Israel's twelve tribes makes 144,000. Many Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers take this as a symbol of God's whole people, complete and kept safe, while others, especially Protestants who read Revelation as a timeline of the end, see a literal group of Jewish believers; the list itself is unusual, with Judah (Jesus' tribe) first and Dan missing, and scholars are unsure why.

parts.label: A crowd no one could count (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: John then sees a crowd too big to count, from every nation and language, wearing white robes and holding palm branches (signs of victory and joy), and they credit their rescue to God and to the Lamb, Revelation's name for Jesus. Some take this crowd to be the 144,000 seen as they really are, and others a second group, believers from every nation alongside those from Israel.

parts.label: The angels worship (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: All the angels stand around the throne and around the elders and four living creatures (heavenly figures from chapter 4), and then the angels fall face down and worship God. Their praise lists seven things, and seven often stands for completeness in Revelation.

parts.label: Who the crowd are (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: An elder explains that they have come out of 'the great tribulation', a time of terrible suffering that some place just before the end and others see as the suffering of believers in John's day or in every age. Their robes were washed white in the Lamb's blood, a deliberate paradox meaning they are made clean through Jesus' death.

parts.label: Sheltered by God (vv. 15-17)
parts.note: They now serve God day and night and he shelters them, where one translation keeps the original picture of God spreading his tent over them. In words borrowed from Isaiah, hunger, thirst and scorching sun are gone, the Lamb becomes their shepherd, and God wipes away every tear.

disagreement: Christians differ over whether the 144,000 and the countless crowd are one people of God described two ways or two distinct groups, and over whether the scene pictures a future end time or God's people through all of history.
think: When someone is in the middle of real suffering, what kind of hope, if any, actually helps them?
